title: Identification of Endoplasmic reticulum Homeostasis-associated diagnostic biomarkers for Sarcopenia through integrated Bioinformatics and Experimental Validation.
authors: Shi, Long; Yan, Hongyu; Lu, Junliang; Yu, Wenkai; Li, Yang; Zhang, Zhiwen
abstract: Sarcopenia is an age-related skeletal muscle disorder characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass and function, yet reliable biomarkers for early diagnosis remain limited. Emerging evidence suggests that disruption of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis contributes to skeletal muscle aging, however, the diagnostic relevance of ER stress- and reticulophagy-related alterations in sarcopenia remains poorly understood. In this study, three skeletal muscle transcriptomic datasets (GSE25941, GSE28422, and GSE38718) were integrated following batch-effect correction to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between sarcopenic and control samples. DEGs were intersected with ER stress and reticulophagy related gene sets to obtain sarcopenia-associated candidate genes. Subsequently, three machine-learning algorithms, including least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), random forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM), were applied to identify key hub genes. Functional enrichment analyses, transcription factor (TF)-miRNA regulatory network construction, protein-chemical interaction analyses, external validation, nomogram development, and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) verification were performed. A total of 236 DEGs were identified, comprising 34 upregulated and 202 downregulated genes. Intersection analysis with 1,772 ER stress and reticulophagy related genes yielded 10 candidate genes, from which five hub genes (ACTC1, NPY, CDKN2B, GADD45G, and GRIA1) were consistently identified by machine-learning analyses. Functional enrichment analysis indicated significant involvement in extracellular matrix organization, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, mitochondrial translation, and respiratory electron transport pathways. Regulatory network analyses further revealed potential interactions with multiple transcription factors, miRNAs, and chemical compounds. In the independent validation cohort (GSE1428), ACTC1 showed strong individual discriminative performance, NPY and GADD45G showed moderate performance, whereas GRIA1 showed limited discrimination and CDKN2B showed near-chance individual performance, whereas the combined gene signature exhibited improved discriminative ability. A predictive nomogram was established. Moreover, qRT-PCR analysis of human skeletal muscle biopsy specimens confirmed significantly increased expression of ACTC1, NPY, CDKN2B, and GRIA1, together with decreased expression of GADD45G in sarcopenic muscle tissues compared with controls (all p < 0.05). Collectively, our findings identified a five-gene signature associated with ER stress and reticulophagy related molecular networks in sarcopenia. Although these genes are not established core regulators of ER stress or reticulophagy, they exhibited promising diagnostic value and may reflect ER homeostasis-related molecular alterations during skeletal muscle aging, providing novel biomarkers and potential insights into the molecular basis of sarcopenia.

title: Tumor-area mitosis proportion as an image-derived mitotic phenotype in lung squamous cell carcinoma: Patient-level prognostic and multi-omics evaluation.
authors: Gunes, Gulcin Yilmaz; Cifci, Mehmet Akif
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mitotic activity is a recognized marker of tumor proliferation, yet its reproducible assessment across whole-slide images (WSIs) remains difficult. We developed a transfer-learning framework for lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) and evaluated whether a patch-derived tumor-area mitosis proportion (TAMP) was associated with survival and molecular tumor characteristics. METHODS: The analysis combined MIDOG 2022 with TCGA-LUSC, including 478 patients and 512 diagnostic WSIs after quality control. Tumor regions and mitotic figures were reviewed by two pathologists with interobserver agreement of Cohen's kappa >/= 0.85. A ResNet-50 model was trained on MIDOG and subsequently adapted to TCGA-LUSC using Focal Loss and stain-aware augmentation. Target-domain performance was evaluated using patient-level stratified 5-fold cross-validation and an additional WSI-level holdout analysis to address potential leakage from the initial patch-level partitioning. TAMP was calculated from patient-level out-of-fold predictions as the proportion of evaluable tumor patches classified as mitosis-positive. Associations with overall survival, immune and genomic features, transcriptomic programs, predicted drug response, and transcription-factor activity were subsequently examined. Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, tumor stage, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status. RESULTS: The model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.975 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.965-0.980) on the held-out MIDOG test set. In TCGA-LUSC, fine-tuning increased the initial patch-level AUC from 0.82 to 0.92. Patient-level cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.86-0.90), and WSI-level holdout validation yielded an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.84-0.90). High TAMP was associated with poorer overall survival (log-rank p = 0.008; HR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.18-2.81) and remained associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.08-2.62; p = 0.022). Higher TAMP was also associated with lower stromal fraction, selected immune-cell differences, greater indel-derived neoantigen load and indel burden, and enrichment of stem-cell proliferation, growth-factor-response, E2F-target, G2M-checkpoint, and MYC-target programs. Additional associations were observed with predicted sensitivity to selected cell-cycle-targeting compounds and with proliferation-related transcription-factor activity. CONCLUSIONS: TAMP provides a patient-level, image-derived representation of mitosis-positive tumor regions that was associated with survival and several molecular features in TCGA-LUSC. Its association with overall survival persisted after adjustment for major clinical covariates. External multicenter validation, prespecified threshold evaluation, and prospective assessment are required before clinical use.

title: The STAT1 lexicon: translating signaling codes in H. pylori-driven gastric carcinogenesis.
authors: Han, Wei; He, Hongzheng; Ye, Bei; Sun, Yilin; Wang, XiuPing; Liu, Tingting; Cui, Hanwei; Wang, Jianjun
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a chronic gastric mucosa colonizer that leads to the Correa cascade of gastric adenocarcinoma progression: chronic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia. Signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) is one of the key mediators at the host immunity-tumor cell interface. The interaction of H. pylori with pattern recognition receptors on gastric epithelial cells induces tyrosine phosphorylation of STAT1 by Janus kinase (JAK), which in turn leads to dimerization and nuclear translocation of the protein, resulting in the suppression of pathogen survival enabled by interferon (IFN)-regulatory transcriptional programs. Ironically, STAT1 has a dual role in gastric carcinogenesis in a context-dependent manner: in the early disease, it acts as a tumor suppressor by facilitating apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest in gastric lesions, but in the advanced disease, it plays a role in immune evasion and tumor progression through the expression of programed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and tumor microenvironment (TME) modulation. This review critically assesses how H. pylori manipulates the STAT1 signaling during the infection process, crosstalk between the STAT1 and STAT3 pathways, and the future use of this understanding to therapeutically target and develop biomarkers. New strategies such as small-molecule STAT inhibitors, combination immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based biomarker discovery are discussed, as well as existing limitations and future research directions.

title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility.
authors: Lee, Jodi; Zhang, Kaite; Shurberg, Ethan; Ramani, Vijay; Pollard, Katherine S
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis -regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

title: Optimization of the NFkappaB-DNA ensemble leads to high affinity binding of partial consensus sites.
authors: Gunther, Tristan R; Hofmeister, Sophia M; Sebastian, Luke; Baughman, Hannah E R; Bethel, Neville; Komives, Elizabeth A
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Our ability to respond to a myriad of external stressors is dependent on the activity of specific transcription factors that precisely regulate gene expression. While some transcription factors have high specificity for their consensus DNA binding site, others such as NFkappaB (RelA/p50) readily bind to partial and nonconsensus sites. In fact, ChIP-Seq data shows that nearly half of the DNA-bound RelA occupies sequences that don't match the consensus. Here we explore how NFkappaB (RelA/p50) binds to alternative sequences that differ subtly from the consensus. The two subunits of the NFkappaB heterodimer, RelA and p50, form an extensive pocket where DNA binding is mediated by both base-specific contacts and nonspecific interactions with the DNA backbone. RelA and p50 each form sequence-specific contacts with DNA at different 4-nucleotide sequences separated by two nucleotides, together forming a 10-base pair consensus binding sequence. Partial consensus sequences, known as "half-sites", match the consensus sequence at only one of these two 4-nucleotide interaction sites. Here, using hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate protein structural dynamics, we observe that rearranging nucleotides at the RelA-interacting end of a consensus DNA sequence to form a half-site induces dynamic structural changes through both subunits of RelA/p50. MD simulations reveal a shift in the position of DNA within the RelA/p50 binding pocket that allows optimal interaction with the half-site sequence. Our results demonstrate how RelA/p50 fine-tunes its interactions to achieve high-affinity binding with multiple different target DNA sequences.

title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor.
authors: Denes, Lance; Emenecker, Ryan J; Wang, Nongyun; Chirumamilla, Devi; Mohotti, Rashmi; Holehouse, Alex S; Holt, Liam; Lionnet, Timothee
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the C-terminal IDR of the transcription factor RUNX2, which is required to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR motifs are dispensable; instead, the conformational dynamics of the IDR predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo . These findings extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

title: SERPINE1 Identifies a Shared Injury-associated Molecular Signature in Intracerebral Hemorrhage and Epilepsy.
authors: Zhang, Xu; Su, Lihan; Zhang, Shijie; Shen, Jing; Yao, Ensheng
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and epilepsy are clinically linked neurological disorders, yet their shared molecular features remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify shared molecular candidates across ICH and epilepsy by integrating transcriptomic data with a curated set of genes with established circadian relevance. Transcriptomic datasets for ICH and epilepsy were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus, and candidate genes were curated from the Molecular Signatures Database and GeneCards. Differentially expressed candidate genes were intersected, and an integrative machine-learning framework-including Boruta, LASSO, XGBoost, and CatBoost-was applied to prioritize shared genes. Integrated machine-learning and network analyses nominated SERPINE1 for further investigation. Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis identified higher scores for porphyrin, folate and pterine, and arachidonic acid metabolism in both disease comparisons. SERPINE1 expression correlated positively with arachidonic acid metabolism scores in both datasets, while Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis linked its expression to inflammatory transcriptional signatures, including TNFA signaling via NFKB and IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling. Gene interaction, drug-mRNA, transcription factor-mRNA, and competing endogenous RNA networks further characterized its regulatory and pharmacological context. Independent bulk transcriptomic datasets and experimental models supported SERPINE1 upregulation, with single-nucleus RNA-sequencing providing complementary cellular context, while single-nucleus analyses and immunostaining further supported its preferential microglial localization. Collectively, these findings identify SERPINE1 as a shared injury-associated molecular feature of ICH and epilepsy, with preferential microglial localization and associations with inflammatory transcriptional signatures and metabolic pathway scores. Although SERPINE1 is known to be clock-regulated, whether its temporal expression pattern is altered in ICH or epilepsy remains to be determined.

title: Harpagide alleviates neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction in sepsis-associated encephalopathy: Association with the MMP9/NF-kappaB signaling pathway.
authors: Lou, Fen; Deng, Guochun; Chen, Jiejuan; Jing, Yijiang; Wang, Ao; Zhang, Mazhong; Zhang, Yongping; Wang, Bin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a severe neurological complication of sepsis, characterized by uncontrolled neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet no specific therapy is currently available. Harpagide, a naturally occurring iridoid glycoside, has been reported to possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective activities; however, its therapeutic potential in SAE remains unexplored. This study aimed to investigate whether Harpagide exerts neuroprotective effects in SAE and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. METHODS: A mouse model of SAE was established by intraperitoneal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 18 mg/kg). Cognitive performance was assessed using behavioral assays. Brain tissue morphology and neuronal survival were evaluated through histopathological examination. Glial cell activation and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) were measured. Network pharmacology was employed to predict potential targets, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations to predict binding interactions with core targets. Western blotting was performed to determine the expression levels of key proteins involved in the MMP9/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. RESULTS: Treatment with Harpagide significantly improved behavioral performance, ameliorated brain pathological changes, preserved hippocampal neurons, suppressed glial activation, and reduced the levels of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 in SAE mice. Network pharmacology analysis predicted four core targets: GAPDH, CASP3, MMP9, and ICAM1. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested stable binding between Harpagide and MMP9. Western blot analysis further showed that Harpagide treatment was associated with reduced expression of MMP9 and phosphorylated NF-kappaB p65 in both hippocampal and cortical tissues. CONCLUSIONS: The present study demonstrates that Harpagide exerts neuroprotective effects in SAE, which are associated with mitigated neuroinflammation and reduced MMP9/NF-kappaB signaling, supporting its potential as a promising therapeutic candidate for this devastating condition.

title: Truncating Kabuki Syndrome-associated KMT2D Mutation in FYR Domain Alters Chromatin Accessibility at Neurodevelopmental Loci.
authors: Ozden-Yilmaz, Gulden; Olmez, Akgun; Yilmazbilek, Irem; Tulu, Ahmet Can; Binokay, Leman; Gencpinar, Pinar; Hiz, Ayse Semra; Oktay, Yavuz; Karakulah, Gokhan; Karaca, Ezgi; Senturk, Serif; Erkek-Ozhan, Serap
abstract: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, developmental delay, and multisystem involvement. KS is primarily caused by de novo mutations in KMT2D, a H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase within the MLL3/4 COMPASS-like complex. Although the role of KMT2D in active chromatin organization is well established, the function of its FYR domain remains largely unknown. Here, we report a KS patient carrying a heterozygous KMT2D p.R5282* nonsense mutation located at the C-terminal side of the FYR domain. The patient exhibited a relatively mild phenotype, consistent with previously reported p.R5282* mutation carriers. ATAC-seq analysis of patient-derived PBMCs revealed 451 differentially accessible regions compared to controls, with reduced accessibility mainly at promoter regions of genes involved in neurogenesis. Motif and regulatory enrichment analyses identified loss of CTCF and WRAD complex components (WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L), suggesting impaired chromatin organization. To examine the functional impact of FYR mutations, we expressed FLAG-tagged KMT2D p.R5282* and another FYR domain hotspot missense mutation (p.R5179C) in HEK293T cells and performed ATAC-seq. p.R5282*-specific chromatin changes mirrored those in the patient and were enriched for promoter regions and WRAD binding sites, whereas p.R5179C showed distinct patterns. AlphaFold3 modeling indicated that p.R5282* truncation disrupts the WIN motif required for WDR5 binding, compromising MLL3/4 complex stability. Both the patient and p.R5282*-expressing cells showed reduced chromatin accessibility at the CHD7 locus, linking KMT2D dysfunction to CHARGE syndrome pathways. These findings highlight the essential role of the KMT2D FYR domain in maintaining WRAD complex integrity and chromatin accessibility.

title: Licoflavone B mitigates allergic rhinitis by restraining epithelial PI3K-AKT/NF-kappaB NLRP3 inflammasome signaling.
authors: Shen, Qi; Ma, Xiaoyao; Liu, Hui; Li, Xuemin; Shao, Wenhui
abstract: Allergic rhinitis remains highly prevalent and is often incompletely controlled by current therapies, while accumulating evidence implicates epithelial PI3K-AKT/NF-kappaB-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in upper-airway inflammation. This study investigated whether the licorice-derived flavonoid Licoflavone B (LFB) alleviates allergic rhinitis by modulating this signaling axis. In an ovalbumin-induced murine model, allergic rhinitis-like symptoms and nasal histopathological changes were evaluated, cytokine levels were quantified by ELISA, and the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and PI3K-AKT/NF-kappaB signaling was assessed by immunoblotting. Unbiased RNA sequencing followed by KEGG and GO enrichment analyses was performed to identify potential upstream pathways. The involvement of PI3K-AKT/NF-kappaB signaling was further explored through PI3K-AKT reactivation with IGF-1 and TLR3 stimulation with poly(I) in vivo and in primary human nasal epithelial cells (HNEpCs). Molecular docking was also conducted to explore the potential interaction between LFB and PI3K. LFB reduced sneezing and nasal scratching, partially ameliorated epithelial thickening and inflammatory-cell infiltration, and decreased mast-cell staining. LFB also reduced the levels of IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-5, IL-13, and TNF-alpha, as well as the expression of NLRP3-inflammasome components. RNA-sequencing analysis identified PI3K-AKT signaling as one of the major enriched pathways, and immunoblotting confirmed that LFB decreased the phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT, and p65 without substantially altering their total protein levels. In HNEpCs, IGF-1 restored pathway phosphorylation and partially reinstated cytokine and inflammasome protein expression, thereby attenuating the effects of LFB. Similarly, IGF-1 or poly(I) partially diminished the symptomatic and histological improvements induced by LFB in vivo. Molecular docking positioned LFB within the PI3K catalytic pocket, providing structural plausibility for a potential LFB-PI3K interaction. Collectively, these findings indicate that LFB alleviates ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis-like inflammation and is associated with reduced activation of the PI3K-AKT/NF-kappaB/NLRP3 signaling axis in nasal tissues, HNEpCs, and stimulated mast-cell models. The partial reversal of these effects by IGF-1 or poly(I) further supports the involvement of this signaling pathway.

title: Explainable hybrid vision transformer-convolutional neural network with cross-attention fusion for multi-institutional breast cancer receptor status prediction from H&E histopathology images.
authors: Albalawi, Elham Saleh; Qayyum, Jibran; Qayyum, Junaid
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital pathology has revolutionised breast cancer diagnostics, offering transformative opportunities to automate and refine molecular profiling, which is essential to precision oncology. Accurate determination of receptor status-estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-remains pivotal in guiding personalised treatment planning and prognostic assessment. However, traditional immunohistochemistry (IHC) and molecular assays are limited by resource intensity, lengthy turnaround times, and inter-observer variability, underscoring the need for scalable computational alternatives. This study proposes a novel integrative AI-driven framework for predicting breast cancer receptor profiles directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathology images. The framework employs a hybrid vision transformer-convolutional neural network (ViT-CNN) architecture with a cross-attention fusion mechanism to capture both global contextual information and fine-grained local features. Experiments show AUCs of 0.967, 0.952, and 0.941 for ER, PR, and HER2 prediction, respectively, representing relative improvements of 12.4%, 9.8%, and 10.8% over the best-performing prior method (DCS-ST), re-evaluated under our identical protocol (absolute AUC differences of 0.107, 0.085 and 0.092). Furthermore, the framework enables automated molecular subtyping into luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, and triple-negative categories with a macro-averaged F1-score of 95.7%. A comprehensive multi-institutional validation was performed on 2,847 external whole-slide images from three partner institutions (not including the primary BINO Hospital test set), showing consistent performance (a mean AUC reduction of 0.83 percentage points relative to the internal test set) across the staining protocols and scanners represented. Integrated explainability modules, including attention visualisations and Grad-CAM, enhance interpretability, supporting pathologist review. In a single-institution retrospective workflow audit, AI assistance was associated with an estimated 72.7% reduction in diagnostic turnaround time (from a conventional mean of 72.4 hours to 19.8 hours; Section 6.10, where approximately 65% of the AI-assisted time is un-itemised queueing and logistics) and, in a 120-WSI reader study, with higher inter-observer agreement (kappa 0.847 to 0.967). These clinical-impact estimates are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation. The findings position the framework as a promising, explainable approach to AI-assisted digital pathology that warrants prospective, multi-centre clinical evaluation.

title: Exploring biomarkers and regulatory mechanisms associated with 20 protein post-translational modifications in acute myocardial infarction based on transcriptomics.
authors: Zhang, Jie; Li, Binhe; Yang, Mengyue; Lu, Jingchao; Jiang, Huiqing; Chen, Fei
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is a critical condition resulting from coronary occlusion, leading to myocardial necrosis and dysfunction. Protein posttranslational modifications (PTMs) regulate key inflammatory and signaling pathways in its pathogenesis. Accordingly, exploring transcriptomic signatures of genes encoding PTM-regulatory factors may provide valuable insights for improving early diagnosis and therapeutic stratification in AMI. METHODS: Candidate genes were obtained by integrating transcriptomic data on AMI from public databases with a previously published gene set encoding regulators for 20 categories of protein PTMs. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were intersected with this PTM-regulator gene set to identify PTM-related DEGs. Machine learning approaches together with expression analyses were employed to identify diagnostic biomarkers. Their potential mechanisms were systematically elucidated via multidimensional analyses, including deep neural network (DNN) model construction, biological pathway analysis, immune landscape profiling, regulatory network reconstruction, and therapeutic compound prioritization. Clinical validation of the key biomarkers was performed using RT-qPCR. RESULTS: This study identified three biomarkers among PTM-regulator-related genes for AMI: GABARAPL1, PELI1, and NLRP3. Enrichment profiling showed that all three biomarkers were prominently linked to pathways related to Leishmania infection. Correlation analysis of immune cell profiles showed that all three biomarkers were most strongly associated with plasmacytoid dendritic cells. Molecular regulatory network analysis uncovered their associated transcription factors, targeted miRNAs, and lncRNA interaction networks. Drug prediction and molecular docking identified several potential targeting compounds, among which 1,4-chrysenequinone exhibited docking scores of -7 kcal/mol and -8.9 kcal/mol with GABARAPL1 and PELI1, respectively, while calcitriol showed a docking score of -10.1 kcal/mol with NLRP3, indicating strong predicted binding affinity. RT-qPCR clinical validation confirmed significant upregulation of GABARAPL1, PELI1, and NLRP3 in AMI patients (all P < 0.01), consistent with the integrative multi-omics findings. CONCLUSION: Using transcriptome-based bioinformatics, this study identified and validated three transcriptomic biomarkers (GABARAPL1, PELI1, and NLRP3) among genes encoding PTM-regulatory factors for AMI, offering molecular resources for future investigations into diagnostic and therapeutic targets in AMI.

title: Identification and validation of RNA-binding protein-associated biomarkers in esophageal cancer.
authors: Gao, Jie; Li, Rizhu; Wu, Xiangsheng; Feng, Xueping
abstract: BACKGROUND: Esophageal cancer (ESCA) is highly prevalent globally, but the role of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) in it remains unclear. METHODS: ESCA datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Candidates were derived by intersecting DEGs with RBP-related genes and validated via machine learning, expression analysis, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Prognostic value, functional enrichment, immune microenvironment, regulatory networks, drug prediction, and Eca-109 cell validation were assessed. RESULTS: Four biomarkers (CDC20, COL7A1, DNMT3B, UBE2T) were confirmed. Low UBE2T/DNMT3B correlated with better survival. In addition, CDC20/UBE2T were linked to DNA replication; COL7A1/DNMT3B to olfactory transduction. Immune analysis showed 15 cell types differed significantly, with most chemokines negatively correlating with biomarkers. CONCLUSIONS: COL7A1, DNMT3B, and UBE2T were associated with transcription factor TET1. The four biomarkers corresponded to 79, 26, 67, and 23 targeted drugs, respectively, and all were highly expressed in Eca-109 cells, advancing insights into RBP-related mechanisms in ESCA.

title: Integrated Computational Pharmacology and Experimental Validation Identify the PLK2-TFEB Axis as a Therapeutic Mechanism of Kunkui Baoshen Decoction in Diabetic Kidney Disease.
authors: Ni, Jing; Zhang, Li; Zhu, Haohan; Yang, Yanjun; Yu, Jiangyi
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Metabolic stress and lipid homeostasis imbalance in proximal tubular cells (PTC) are increasingly recognized as critical contributors to diabetic kidney disease (DKD) progression, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Kunkui Baoshen Decoction (KKBS) has shown clinical benefits in DKD, but its molecular basis remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the therapeutic targets and regulatory mechanisms of KKBS in DKD-associated proximal tubular injury. METHODS: An integrated multi-omics strategy combining network pharmacology, transcriptomic analysis, machine learning, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was applied to identify candidate therapeutic targets of KKBS in DKD. Then, the protective effects of KKBS were further evaluated in db/db mice and high-glucose and high-lipid (HGHL)-induced HK-2 cells by assessing renal function, lipid metabolism, autophagic flux, transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation, and fibrosis-related markers. RESULTS: KKBS effectively reduced urinary protein excretion, corrected aberrant lipid metabolism, and mitigated renal fibrotic lesions in db/db mice. Integrated multi-omics profiling highlighted polo-like kinase 2 (PLK2) as a potential therapeutic target, and scRNA-seq analysis demonstrated its progressive upregulation in PTC during DKD progression. Mechanistically, KKBS treatment reduced PLK2 expression, restored TFEB nuclear translocation, improved autophagic flux, and decreased lipid droplet accumulation. Similar effects were reproduced by PLK2 inhibition in HGHL-induced HK-2 cells. DISCUSSION: These findings support the PLK2-TFEB axis as a potential therapeutic target in DKD. CONCLUSION: KKBS may alleviate lipid accumulation and fibrotic alterations in DKD by suppressing PLK2 expression, facilitating TFEB nuclear translocation, and restoring autophagy-lysosome-related function.

title: Integrative transcriptomic and single-cell analysis identifies a manganese-associated transcriptional signature and a potential JUN/HBEGF-associated endothelial signature in COPD pulmonary vascular remodeling.
authors: Liu, Ziyi; Nie, Li; Zeng, Huihui
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a heterogeneous respiratory disease involving airway inflammation, emphysema, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. Manganese exposure has been linked to pulmonary inflammation and oxidative stress, but its molecular association with COPD vascular pathology remains unclear. This study explored a manganese-associated transcriptional signature in COPD and investigated its potential relationship with endothelial cell dysfunction and vascular remodeling. METHODS: Bulk transcriptomic datasets were used to calculate a manganese-related transcriptional score, identify differentially expressed genes, and characterize WGCNA modules. Manganese-COPD-associated genes were obtained by intersecting manganese-related genes, COPD differentially expressed genes, and manganese-associated module genes. Functional enrichment, PPI analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, diagnostic modeling, and consensus clustering were performed. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed to characterize HBEGF expression, endothelial subpopulations, CytoTRACE2 scores, pseudotime dynamics, transcription factor activity, cell-cell communication, and NicheNet ligand-target relationships. RESULTS: COPD samples showed significantly higher manganese-related transcriptional scores. A total of 43 manganese-COPD-associated candidate genes were identified and were enriched mainly in pathways related to inflammation, cytokines, immune chemotaxis, and vascular processes. Machine learning identified 14 core diagnostic genes, and the combined model showed good classification performance in the training and validation cohorts. Among these genes, HBEGF showed the highest contribution in the ElasticNet model and was prioritized for downstream analysis. Consensus clustering divided COPD samples into two molecular subtypes with distinct manganese-related scores and functional features. Single-cell analysis suggested that HBEGF was closely associated with endothelial cell alterations, especially venous endothelial cells. Pseudotime and transcription factor analyses suggested a potential JUN/HBEGF regulatory relationship. CellChat and NicheNet analyses further indicated that venous endothelial cell-derived HBEGF may participate in endothelial-smooth muscle cell communication. CONCLUSION: This study identified an elevated manganese-related transcriptional score in COPD and prioritized HBEGF as a key candidate associated with venous endothelial cell state changes and endothelial-smooth muscle communication. These findings suggest a potential JUN/HBEGF-associated endothelial signature relevant to COPD pulmonary vascular remodeling, which warrants further experimental validation.

title: Rotigotine Attenuates Mechanical Hypersensitivity in 6-OHDA-Lesioned Rats: Associations with D2/D3 Receptors and Spinal Glial NF-kappaB/p65 Signaling.
authors: Santamaria-Anzures, Jazmin; Martinez-Lorenzana, Guadalupe; Gonzalez-Morales, Estefania; Palmeros-Barreda, Dafne; De-la-Cruz-Martinez, Ledy; Cortes-Benitez, Francisco; Perez-Ramos, Julia; Condes-Lara, Miguel; Godinez-Chaparro, Beatriz
abstract: Pain is a debilitating non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD). This study investigated whether rotigotine attenuated pain hypersensitivity (allodynia and hyperalgesia) in hemiparkinsonian rats and explored D1/D2/D3 receptor involvement, NF-kappaB/p-p65 signaling modulation in glial cells, and spinal TNF-alpha and IL-1beta expression. The PD model was induced by unilateral 6-OHDA injection into the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc). Pain sensitivity was assessed using von Frey filaments. Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence were used to analyze tyrosine hydroxylase levels in the SNpc and striatum, GFAP, Iba-1, and NF-kappaB/p-p65 expression in the dorsal horn of the L5 spinal cord, and ELISA was used to determine TNF-alpha and IL-1beta levels in the lumbar spinal cord. Both acute (8 h) and subacute (5-day) intranasal rotigotine (0.1, 0.5, 0.75, and 1 mg/kg) showed antiallodynic and antihyperalgesic effects. These effects were prevented by selective D2 (L-741,626; 14.6 nmol) and D3 (nafadotride; 3 nmol) receptor antagonists, but not by the D1 receptor antagonist SCH-23,390 (30 nmol). Subacute rotigotine was associated with reduced 6-OHDA-induced glial activation, decreased NF-kappaB/p-p65 expression, and attenuated spinal TNF-alpha and IL-1beta levels. Molecular docking suggests a potential interaction between rotigotine and the p65 subunit of NF-kappaB, with favorable binding energy. In conclusion, rotigotine moderated PD-related pain, potentially through D2/D3 receptor activation and modulation of neuroinflammation. This suggested antinociceptive effect may be linked to suppressing glial activation and inhibiting spinal astrocytes' NF-kappaB/p-p65 signaling, potentially reducing subsequent proinflammatory cytokine release. These findings suggest that rotigotine may represent a promising therapeutic option for managing sensory hypersensitivity in PD.

title: Inulin Combined with Rosmarinic Acid Alleviates D-Galactose-Induced Cognitive Impairment by Regulating Indoxyl Sulfate and the AhR/NF-kappaB/NLRP3 Inflammatory Pathway.
authors: Xu, Huajian; Xu, Jinghong; Li, Zheng; Zhang, Qing; Che, Jing; Yi, Haozhe; Zhang, Binjia; Li, Bowen
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Age-related cognitive impairment is associated with oxidative stress, intestinal barrier dysfunction, and gut-brain axis disruption. This study evaluated how rosmarinic acid (RA), alone or combined with the prebiotic inulin, ameliorates D-galactose-induced cognitive impairment in mice. Male ICR mice received D-galactose for 6 weeks with RA, or RA plus inulin, followed by behavioral testing, histology, biochemical assays, 16S rRNA sequencing, serum metabolomics, molecular dynamics and inflammatory signaling analyses. RA ameliorated exploratory behavior and recognition and spatial memory, restored antioxidant enzyme (SOD/CAT/GSH-Px) activities, reduced lipid peroxidation (MDA), and attenuated hippocampal neuronal injury and glial activation. The RA-inulin combination exhibited additional protection, improving colonic barrier markers, increasing Lactobacillus and Lachnospiraceae, lowering indoxyl sulfate, and modulating AhR/NF-kappaB/NLRP3 activation. Meanwhile, the level of IL-1beta/IL-18 (in the hippocampus) decreased by 15.96% and 24.41%, respectively. These findings suggest that the combined dietary intervention of RA and inulin mitigates aging-related cognitive impairment through the gut-brain axis.

title: Allobaculum stercoricanis and Its Postbiotics Alleviate Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-Induced Colitis through the Regulation of theTLR4/NF-kappaB Signaling Pathway.
authors: Wang, Teng; Wang, Jiantang; Huangfu, Bingxin; He, Xiaoyun; Huang, Kunlun
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disorder that has become a global public health concern. Postbiotics offer advantages in biosafety and reproducibility over probiotics. Here, we demonstrated that live Allobaculum stercoricanis (A. stercoricanis) and its two postbiotic preparations horizontal line inactivated bacterial cells (POST) and cell-free fermentation supernatant (CFS) horizontal line effectively alleviated dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. Integrated gut microbiome and serum metabolomics analyses indicated that these interventions may act through modulating bile acid metabolism and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways. Further investigations combining postbiotic metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations identified alpha-muricholic acid (alpha-MCA) as a candidate functional metabolite, with the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) as a potential target. We hypothesize that alpha-MCA may contribute to ameliorating intestinal inflammation through engagement of FXR and suppression of the TLR4/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. These findings provide new insights into postbiotic-based therapeutic strategies for IBD.

title: UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS Identification of Intestinal Absorbable Components of Yindan Pinggan Capsule and Exploration of Its Anti-NAFLD Mechanism Based on NF-kappaB Signaling Regulation.
authors: Hou, Jinli; Zhao, Jie; Yang, Jicheng; Lai, Huaqing; Jia, Mengyu; Song, Wenrui; Han, Yutong; Li, Sen; Wu, Hongwei
abstract: Yindan Pinggan capsule (YDPG) is a traditional Chinese formula for liver disorders, but its mechanism against nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) remains unclear. Here, UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS was used to characterize YDPG's chemical profile, and the YDPG intestinal absorption solution (YDPGIAS) obtained via the everted gut sac model was analyzed to identify absorbable components. Network pharmacology, transcriptomic sequencing, molecular docking, and in vitro assays in oleic acid-induced BRL-3A hepatocytes were integrated to predict targets and validate effects. A total of 164 compounds were identified from YDPG; 84 were detected in YDPGIAS, with 15 confirmed by reference standards. YDPGIAS significantly reduced lipid accumulation and lowered triglyceride, total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and HDL-cholesterol levels. Integrated analysis identified the NF-kappaB pathway as the core candidate mechanism, involving targets LYN, TNF, and IL1B, and key compounds including baicalin, ferulic acid, and gentiopicroside. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding affinities, and cellular experiments confirmed lipid-lowering effects. These results demonstrate that YDPG ameliorates NAFLD through multicomponent, multitarget regulation of the NF-kappaB-mediated inflammatory pathway, providing a preliminary basis for further pharmacological and clinical investigation in NAFLD management.

title: Identification and Validation of Autophagy- and Inflammatory-Related Genes in Childhood Asthma via Integrated Bioinformatics and Clinical Samples.
authors: Huang, Mingjing; Wu, Jihua; Xu, Daliang
abstract: Childhood asthma (CA) is a prevalent chronic airway disease, yet the roles of autophagy and inflammation in its pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Transcriptomic datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Inflammation- and autophagy-related genes were identified using weighted gene co-expression network analysis and consensus clustering and intersected with differentially expressed genes (DEGs) to identify candidate genes. Subsequently, 101 machine learning algorithm combinations were evaluated to select key genes for diagnostic model construction. Functional characterization involved immune infiltration analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, and transcription factor network construction. Mendelian randomization (MR) was used to assess potential causal relationships between key genes and CA, and gene expression was validated by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in clinical blood samples. The analysis identified 39 candidate genes associated with autophagy and inflammation. Machine learning identified 10 key genes, and the resulting diagnostic model achieved areas under the curve of 0.768, 0.751, and 0.710 in the training, test, and validation sets, respectively. Pathway and immune infiltration analyses revealed enrichment in signaling, metabolic, and immune-regulatory functions and significant correlations with immune cell infiltration. MR analysis suggested a potential causal association between genetically predicted STYXL1 expression and CA risk. qPCR analysis in five CA patients and five healthy controls showed expression patterns consistent with the transcriptomic findings. However, the small clinical validation cohort limits the generalizability of these results. This study identifies a 10-gene peripheral blood diagnostic signature associated with CA and highlights STYXL1 as a potential causal risk gene supported by genetic evidence. Larger clinical cohorts and functional studies are required to validate these findings.

title: Integrative Transcriptomic and Network Analyses Reveal Common Molecular Signatures and Turmeric-Derived Common Therapeutic Candidates for Neurological Diseases.
authors: Bayragi, Sumi Rani; Hossain, Riday; Islam, Md Zohurul; Sumi, Sharmin Akter; Ahmed, Fee Faysal
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurological diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), stroke, and brain tumors, impose a substantial global health burden. Although these disorders have distinct clinical manifestations and etiologies, accumulating evidence suggests that they share certain molecular mechanisms. However, their common molecular signatures and the therapeutic potential of turmeric-derived bioactive compounds have not been systematically investigated. OBJECTIVES: This study is aimed at identifying shared molecular mechanisms and key hub genes across AD, PD, stroke, and glioblastoma (GBM) using an integrative bioinformatics framework and at investigating turmeric-derived compounds as potential multitarget common therapeutic candidates. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Gene expression datasets (GSE22491, GSE5281, GSE122709, and GSE4290) were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Common host differentially expressed genes (cHDEGs) were identified through integrated bioinformatics analysis. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were subsequently constructed to identify common hub genes (cHubGs), followed by functional enrichment and transcription factor (TF) and miRNA-mediated regulatory network analyses. The interactions between the identified cHubGs and turmeric-derived compounds were further investigated using molecular docking and 500-ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS). RESULTS: A total of 81 cHDEGs and four cHubGs (CCNB1, CDK1, CYCS, and STAT3) were identified. Functional enrichment and regulatory network analysis revealed shared biological processes and signaling pathways, as well as key TFs and miRNAs potentially associated with ND pathogenesis. Among the 77 turmeric-derived compounds that passed the toxicity screening, demethoxycurcumin, cyclocurcumin, and (1E,4E)-1-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)-5-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-1,4-pentadien-3-one exhibited the strongest predicted binding affinities. The selected compound-target complexes also showed stable behavior during the MDS. CONCLUSION: This study provides insights into the shared molecular features across AD, PD, stroke, and GBM and prioritizes turmeric-derived compounds as potential multitarget therapeutic candidates. These computational findings require further validation through independent datasets and experimental studies.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic Analysis and Experimental Validation Identify ATF3 as a Mesangial Cell-Associated Candidate Regulator in IgA Nephropathy.
authors: Liang, Mingzhu; Gan, Xinyu; Shadekejiang, Halinuer; Hong, Huan; Li, Xu; Xia, Ting; Wang, Jie; Zhang, Xueqin; Lu, Chen
abstract: BACKGROUND: IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is an immune-mediated glomerular disease marked by mesangial proliferation, inflammation, extracellular matrix accumulation, and progressive renal injury. This study aimed to identify IgAN-associated genes and evaluate the relevance of activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) to mesangial cell activation. METHODS: Public bulk transcriptomic datasets were integrated for differential expression, co-expression network, machine learning, and immune infiltration analyses. Single-cell RNA sequencing, mesangial cell-specific high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and single-cell regulatory network inference were used to assess cell type-specific expression and regulatory activity. The findings were further evaluated using Nephroseq and an aggregated IgA1-stimulated human mesangial cell model with ATF3 knockdown. RESULTS: Integrated analysis identified 47 shared differentially expressed genes and a 12-gene candidate set with reduced expression in IgAN. ATF3 was prioritized as a mesangial cell-associated candidate and showed reduced expression and regulon activity in the analyzed single-cell dataset. Nephroseq analysis showed lower glomerular ATF3 expression in IgAN-related kidney disease samples; ATF3 expression was positively associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate and negatively associated with serum creatinine and proteinuria. Aggregated IgA1 reduced ATF3 expression in human mesangial cells, whereas ATF3 knockdown further increased inflammatory cytokine expression and proliferative activity. CONCLUSION: Reduced ATF3 expression is associated with IgAN-related mesangial cell activation. ATF3 may represent a mesangial cell-associated candidate regulator that warrants further mechanistic and clinical validation.

title: Computational identification of EBNA1-binding candidates using machine learning-based virtual screening and molecular docking.
authors: Pauskar, Akshata P; Natarajan, Elamathi
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with several malignancies and multiple sclerosis, and Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) plays an essential role in viral genome replication and episome maintenance. The experimentally characterized KVD-associated pocket within the EBNA1 DNA-binding domain provides a structurally defined site for computational ligand prioritization. This study aimed to identify and prioritize predicted EBNA1-binding candidates using an integrated machine-learning and structure-based virtual screening framework. A PubChem EBNA1 bioactivity dataset comprising 304,124 records was curated to obtain 4,584 unique compounds. Molecular representation combined 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints with 11 RDKit molecular descriptors. Random Forest, SVM-RBF, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost models were evaluated using scaffold-based independent testing. The optimized XGBoost model was applied to a non-overlapping DrugBank library of 12,287 compounds. Compounds with predicted activity probabilities >/=0.5 were subjected to Lipinski-based filtering, followed by molecular docking against the KVD-associated binding pocket of EBNA1 (PDB ID: 6NPM). Docking validation was performed by independent KVD redocking at exhaustiveness values of 8, 16, and 32. Post-docking candidates were further evaluated using PAINS, aggregation, frequent-hitter/promiscuity, assay-interference, redox-associated structural-alert, and ADMET assessments. XGBoost demonstrated the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.835), PR-AUC (0.408), and best Brier score (0.067), and was selected for virtual screening. Screening identified 116 compounds above the probability threshold, of which 40 satisfied Lipinski criteria and were docked. Thirty-two compounds achieved docking scores </= -7.0 kcal/mol. Sequential liability assessment and integrated prioritization identified 10 computationally prioritized EBNA1-binding candidates with favorable combined machine-learning, docking, and structural-filter profiles. The integrated computational framework enabled systematic prioritization of structurally diverse predicted EBNA1-binding candidates for further experimental investigation. The identified candidates represent computationally prioritized molecules for subsequent biochemical and functional evaluation of EBNA1 binding and activity and should not be interpreted as experimentally validated antiviral or disease-modifying agents. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT: Virtual screening for drug discovery using trained ML model for EBNA1 protein, Molecular Docking, and ADMET analysis.

title: Nutrigenomics in Dairy Cattle: Causes and Implications.
authors: Tamasgen, Negasa; Asefa, Bacha
abstract: Nutrigenomics is a rapidly developing interdisciplinary field that investigates the interactions between nutrients and the genome, with particular emphasis on how dietary components regulate gene expression and metabolic pathways. In dairy cattle, nutrigenomics has gained increasing attention due to its potential to improve milk production, metabolic efficiency, health, reproduction, and overall animal performance. Nutrients and bioactive dietary compounds can influence gene activity directly through transcriptional regulation or indirectly through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA-mediated gene regulation. These nutrigenomic interactions affect important biological processes including lipid metabolism, adipogenesis, immune response, mammary gland development, and milk synthesis. Advances in omics technologies including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and next-generation sequencing have enhanced understanding of the molecular responses of dairy cows to nutritional interventions. Dietary fatty acids, vitamins, methyl donors, and short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate have been shown to regulate key transcription factors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), sterol regulatory element binding proteins (SREBPs), and liver X receptors (LXRs), thereby modulating metabolic and physiological functions. Nutritional interventions, feed restriction, and supplementation produce tissue-specific molecular responses in the liver, adipose tissue, mammary gland, and immune system, demonstrating interaction between diet, physiological state, and metabolic regulation. Despite these advances, challenges with genetic and physiological variability, tissue-specific responses, integration of multi-omics data, and translation of molecular findings into practical feeding strategies remain unresolved. Future integration of nutrigenomics with microbiome research, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and precision livestock technologies may facilitate nutritional strategies to improve dairy cattle health, productivity, feed efficiency, and product quality.

title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root.
authors: Denyer, Tom; Solansky, Pavel; Herrmann, Arvid; de Martino, Francesco; Symeonidi, Efthymia; Brosamle, Valentin; Timmermans, Marja C P
abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging.
authors: Cheng, Xiu-Tang; Gao, Yifei; Chan, Chung Yu; Xie, Yuxiang; Dai, Yuanyi; Xiong, Gui-Jing; Sathler, Alexandre R; Roney, Joseph C; Li, Sunan; Li, Yan; Wu, Ling-Gang; Sheng, Zu-Hang
abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis reveals a GALNT6/Smad2/CDC7 axis promoting cisplatin resistance through enhanced DNA damage repair in bladder cancer.
authors: Liu, Yang; Bian, Ziming; Hu, Jianting; Xie, Yuanxin; Cheng, Guanyu; Zhang, Yan; Fan, Sairong; Chen, Xiaoming
abstract: Cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy remains an important treatment for advanced bladder cancer (BLCA), yet approximately half of patients derive limited benefit because of chemoresistance. Although DNA damage repair (DDR) is a key determinant of this resistance, how DDR heterogeneity contributes to chemoresistance remains unclear. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed DDR heterogeneity among BLCA epithelial cells, with epithelial cells exhibiting higher DDR activity showing greater malignant potential. Bulk transcriptomic and proteomic analyses identified two molecular subtypes of BLCA. Compared with the DDR-Base subtype, the DDR-Active subtype exhibited enhanced DDR function and worse clinical outcomes. Integrative machine-learning modeling and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) prioritized GALNT6 as a glycosylation-related regulator associated with the DDR-Active phenotype. GALNT6 was highly expressed in the DDR-Active subtype and progressively increased along the epithelial-cell trajectory toward the DDR-enhanced malignant state. Functionally, GALNT6 knockdown impaired DNA damage repair efficiency, thereby overcoming cisplatin resistance in BLCA. Mechanistically, GALNT6 stabilized SMAD2 through O-glycosylation, after which SMAD2 transcriptionally activated CDC7 to enhance repair capacity against exogenous DNA damage. Moreover, GALNT6 and SMAD2 co-expression was a hallmark of the DDR-Active subtype and was associated with advanced tumor stage. This study defines clinically relevant DDR subtypes in BLCA and identifies the GALNT6/SMAD2/CDC7 axis as a driver of cisplatin resistance. These findings provide a biological framework for understanding heterogeneity in cisplatin response and for future treatment stratification.

title: Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions drive chromatin compartmentalization.
authors: Ostwal, Yogesh; Muzzopappa, Fernando; Heurteau, Alexandre; Raffel, Raoul; Veluchamy, Alaguraj; Eswara, Karthik; Boudellioua, Ahlem; Ali, Shakila; Kumari, Reema; Depierre, David; Vadlamani, Satya; Schickele, Naomi; Schaak, Stephane; Erdel, Fabian; Cuvier, Olivier; Fischle, Wolfgang
abstract: The chromatin components that are involved in organizing eukaryotic genomes into active and inactive compartments remain unclear. In analysing viable Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking different chromatin-regulatory proteins, we found that the HP1-type factor HPL-2 and the MBT-domain protein LIN-61 jointly contribute to chromatin compartmentalization. Genomic regions bound by both proteins and their cognate histone mark H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) form broad interfaces of 30-50 kilobases that engage in combinatorial interactions, which we term 'Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions' (VELCROs). Remarkably, VELCROs are defined by high density of H3K9me2, HPL-2, and LIN-61 sites, but not by the intensity of their individual peaks. Mutants that display defective chromatin compartmentalization are impaired in VELCROs. Polymer simulations show that VELCROs can drive a phase transition that segregates B from A chromatin compartments depending on peak densities. Our work identifies VELCROs as stochastic ensembles of interactions constrained within defined chromatin hubs that shape genome compartmentalization.

title: Integrative Analysis of Epidermal Barrier Dysfunction Regulators in Psoriasis.
authors: Liu, Yingdi; Wang, Yinglin; Zhu, Haijun; Liu, Yang; Wang, Jinyan; Li, Fangfang; Zhang, Yuxin; Peng, Zhanli; Wang, Wenxin
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation and compromised epidermal barrier function. Although tight junction disruption is a key pathological hallmark, the upstream transcriptional mechanisms driving the downregulation of core barrier proteins such as claudin-1 (CLDN1) remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: We implemented an integrative multi-omics framework combining weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and machine-learning algorithms to prioritize core diagnostic features in psoriasis. Upstream transcription factors regulating CLDN1 were computationally predicted using the JASPAR, hTFtarget, and KnockTF databases. The regulatory effect of E74-like ETS transcription factor 3 (ELF3) on the CLDN1 promoter was evaluated using dual-luciferase reporter assays, and the inflammatory response of the axis was examined in TNF-alpha-stimulated HaCaT keratinocytes via quantitative real-time PCR. RESULTS: Machine-learning prioritization identified CLDN1 as a robust diagnostic feature that is significantly downregulated in psoriatic lesions. Multi-database integration converged on ELF3 as a candidate negative regulator of CLDN1. Dual-luciferase reporter assays demonstrated that ELF3 overexpression significantly suppressed wild-type CLDN1 promoter activity, whereas mutation of the predicted binding site abolished this repression. In TNF-alpha-stimulated HaCaT cells, ELF3 was markedly upregulated with a concurrent downregulation of CLDN1. DISCUSSION : These findings suggest that ELF3 functions as a candidate transcriptional repressor of CLDN1 promoter activity and provide preliminary in vitro and computational insights into the transcriptional alterations associated with epidermal barrier disruption in psoriasis, highlighting potential avenues for restoring structural barrier integrity.

title: AI and computational methods for reconstructing cell-state-specific gene regulatory networks from single-cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data in cancer: methods, applications, and perspectives.
authors: Wang, Jinying; Chen, Fenjuan
abstract: Tumor heterogeneity is shaped by genetic, epigenetic, microenvironmental, and stochastic factors, among which cell-state-specific regulatory programs are a major determinant. Gene regulatory networks provide a systems-level model linking transcription factors, cis-regulatory elements, and target genes. Paired single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq) measure chromatin accessibility and gene expression in the same cell, offering a direct view of regulatory elements and transcriptional output; matched-but-unpaired, imputed, and single-modality designs can extend coverage but introduce additional assumptions and artifacts. This mini-review focuses on AI and computational methods for reconstructing cell-state-specific GRNs from single-cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data in cancer. We define inclusion criteria, distinguish same-cell paired, matched-unpaired, imputed, and single-modality designs, and organize methods by inference objective and input requirement. We cover motif/co-accessibility inference, deep integration and graph learning, dynamic and cell-state-specific modeling, and virtual perturbation. We then discuss applications in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, treatment resistance, lineage plasticity, and tumor subtyping, emphasizing an evidence hierarchy from statistical association to directional prediction, in silico perturbation, and experimentally supported causal regulation. Finally, we examine benchmarking, limitations, and translational prospects. These approaches may help convert GRNs from descriptive maps into testable models of tumor regulation, but clinical utility still requires prospective validation.

title: A Dual Mechanism-Based Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Model for Predicting Mitoxantrone and Liposomal Mitoxantrone Disposition: Preclinical Validation in Rats and Human Extrapolation with Clinical Evaluation.
authors: Xu, Yuxiang; Li, Shuo; Yang, Zhixuan; Qiu, Yushuo; Dong, Jiameng; Gao, Xiaonan; Gao, Jinglin; Feng, Zhangying; Wang, Mingxia
abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to develop a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to quantitatively predict plasma and tissue concentrations of both liposomal-encapsulated and free mitoxantrone in rats and further extrapolate the model to human clinical scenarios. METHODS: A dual-compartment PBPK framework was constructed to separately describe the disposition of liposomal carriers and released free mitoxantrone. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) based on partial rank correlation coefficient (PRCC) was performed to identify key parameters. The external validation was evaluated using rat plasma pharmacokinetic and human clinical data from previous reported studies. Allometric scaling was applied to extrapolate the model to adult humans, and Monte Carlo simulation was utilized to predict clinical plasma concentrations under fixed clinical doses of 20, 30, and 40 mg in lymphoma patients. RESULTS: PRCC analysis results demonstrated that tissue DNA binding capacity (T_DNA) and tissue-to-plasma liposome partition coefficient (Kp_n) were the most dominant parameters governing free drug and liposomal exposure, respectively (PRCC > 0.9). Overall average absolute fold error (AAFE) for tissue predictions was below 2.0. A slightly higher AAFE of 2.16 was observed for free drug submodel, which still complied with the widely accepted 3-fold error threshold for PBPK validation. Model external validation results also demonstrated acceptable predictive capacity of the model for both total and free mitoxantrone concentrations across preclinical and clinical dose levels (AAFE < 3). For human extrapolation, over 92% of clinically observed plasma concentrations from 37 lymphoma patients fell within the model's 90% predictive interval. CONCLUSION: This study established a robust, mechanism-driven PBPK model that distinguished encapsulated and free mitoxantrone disposition. The model achieved reliable prediction performance and effectively interprets pharmacokinetic characteristics of PEGylated liposomal mitoxantrone. The present framework provided a valuable mechanistic reference for the construction and optimization of liposomal mitoxantrone PBPK models and supported future translational pharmacokinetic studies of liposomal formulations.

title: Cardamonin attenuates SH-SY5Y neuronal apoptosis induced by LPS-activated microglia via modulation of the EGFR/PI3K/AKT1/ERK/NF-kappaB pathway.
authors: Lu, Jingjing; Zhou, Rong; Tang, Kechao; Wang, Hangwei; Shen, Zhongxia; Huang, Chao; Cui, Lijun
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Microglial activation-induced neuroinflammation plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases. Cardamonin (CD, 2',4'-dihydroxy-6'-methoxychalcone), a natural chalcone flavonoid present in several medicinal plants, demonstrates significant anti-inflammatory activity. Nevertheless, the precise mechanisms by which it mitigates neuroinflammation remain incompletely understood. METHODS: In this study, the potential targets and pathways of CD were investigated using network pharmacology and molecular docking. The neuroinflammatory protective mechanisms were examined in vitro using LPS-stimulated BV2 cells and a BV2/SH-SY5Y co-culture system, employing ELISA, RT-qPCR, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and other assays. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Network pharmacology identified epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), rac-alpha serine/threonine-protein kinase (AKT1), heat shock protein 90 alpha family class B member 1 (HSP90AB1), prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2/COX-2) and transcription factor p65 (RELA) as key potential targets, with the EGFR/PI3K/AKT1, MAPK/ERK, and NF-kappaB signaling pathways being the main enriched pathways. In BV2 cells, CD suppressed LPS-induced production of IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, and nitric oxide (NO), and modulated the EGFR/PI3K/AKT1/ERK/NF-kappaB signaling axis. Pharmacological inhibition of EGFR or PI3K phenocopied the effects of CD, supporting the functional involvement of this pathway. Additionally, CD attenuated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and prevented the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential. In a co-culture model, CD pretreatment reduced BV2-conditioned medium neurotoxicity toward SH-SY5Y neurons. Collectively, these findings suggest that CD alleviates neuroinflammation through modulation of the EGFR/PI3K/AKT1/ERK/NF-kappaB pathway, mitigating inflammatory and oxidative stress responses and providing indirect neuroprotection, supporting its potential application in neuroinflammation-associated neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Identification of YL064 as a novel inhibitor of ATXN3 to suppress tumor growth and metastasis by promoting degradation of oncogenic substrates.
authors: Zhang, Zhenge; Bai, Wenhui; Tan, Yayue; Li, Guanyi; Zhang, Youping; Wu, Wenxuan; Zhu, Chujiao; Liu, Xingyu; Zhang, Manyu; Lei, Hu; Xu, Hanzhang; Yang, Li; Liu, Ligen; Zhao, Yaxue; Yao, Zhujun; Zhu, Qi; Wang, Yingying; Wu, Yingli
abstract: ATXN3 has recently emerged as a pro-oncogenic deubiquitinating enzyme (DUB) involved in the progression of multiple cancers, including breast and prostate cancer. However, the therapeutic potential of targeting ATXN3 remains largely unexplored due to the lack of effective inhibitors. In this study, we performed an Ub-AMC-based high-throughput screening assay using full-length ATXN3 and identified YL064, a derivative of the natural product sinomenine isolated from Sinomenium acutum, as a novel ATXN3 inhibitor. Direct interaction between YL064 and ATXN3 was confirmed by thermal shift assay, cellular thermal shift assay, surface plasmon resonance, and molecular docking analysis. Functionally, YL064 suppressed cancer cell proliferation, induced cell-cycle arrest, and reduced metastatic potential. Mechanistically, YL064 inhibited ATXN3 deubiquitinating activity and promoted the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of ATXN3 substrates, including KLF4 and YAP. Furthermore, YL064 significantly inhibited tumor growth in an orthotopic breast cancer model in vivo. Collectively, our findings establish YL064 as a promising ATXN3 inhibitor that targets the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway to exert anti-tumor effects, highlighting its potential as a novel therapeutic agent for ATXN3-driven cancers.

title: Identification of potential regulators of caffeine biosynthesis in shading- and nano‑selenium-treated tea leaves based on integrated bioinformatics and AlphaFold3 analysis.
authors: Ye, Jianhui; Han, Qianou; Zhu, Jin; Li, Chunyang
abstract: Caffeine is an important flavor and bioactive compound in tea, yet external stimuli-induced regulatory networks of caffeine biosynthesis remain largely unclear. Our study showed that shading and nano‑selenium (SeNPs) treatments respectively increased caffeine content in tea leaves from 35.96 mg/g to approximately 43 mg/g, whereas their combined treatment exerted a synergistic effect, raising it to 51.12 mg/g. Correlation of transcriptome with caffeine content and treatment factors via WGCNA and Mantel tests identified 4 key gene modules and 64 transcription factors (TFs). To accelerate TF screening, we established a rapid and high-throughput screening strategy by integrating AlphaFold3 with JASPAR motif prediction, resulting in 10 candidate TF-DNA complexes. Subsequent validation in yeast and tobacco systems confirmed that CsTSO1 directly binds to the promoter of CsSAMS. Our study uncovers how shading and SeNPs modulate caffeine biosynthesis in tea plants, and provide an AI-assisted framework for efficient TF screening in plant metabolic network.

title: Super-enhancers: regulatory mechanisms, biological functions, diseases, and therapeutic targets.
authors: Miao, Huijie; Liu, Yuanding; Yang, Kaini; Gu, Ao; Zhang, Cuifeng; Li, Mengyao; Wang, Jie
abstract: Super-enhancers (SEs) are operationally defined as clusters of cis-regulatory elements associated with high transcriptional activity and cell-identity genes. They display dense transcription factor and coactivator occupancy, strong H3K27 acetylation, and enhancer-promoter communication, but their annotation varies across platforms, algorithms, and thresholds. This review examines SE architecture, identification, and validation, distinguishing chromatin-based annotation from functional dependence demonstrated by locus-specific perturbations. Mechanisms of SE-associated transcription include pioneer factors, chromatin remodelers, three-dimensional genome organization, transcriptional condensates, non-coding RNAs, and extrachromosomal DNA. Physiological functions in development, immunity, and metabolic homeostasis are considered alongside context-dependent dysregulation in cancer, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and metabolic diseases. Breast cancer provides a model for examining subtype-specific regulation and transcriptional plasticity. Particular attention is given to enhancer remodeling during endocrine therapy, cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibition, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted treatment, and chemotherapy, which may support bypass signaling, stemness, and persistent resistance. Causal regulatory changes must nevertheless be distinguished from correlates of treatment selection. Therapeutic approaches targeting bromodomain and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins, CDK7/9, chromatin regulators, enhancer RNAs, and regulatory loci are critically evaluated. Definitional uncertainty, model dependence, limited reproducibility, systemic toxicity, and insufficient clinical validation remain major barriers. Priorities include standardized annotation, temporally resolved perturbation, single-cell and spatial profiling, artificial intelligence-assisted integration, patient-derived models, and biomarker-guided therapeutic development. Together, these perspectives position SEs as a context-dependent framework linking regulatory architecture to disease progression and treatment resistance, while emphasizing the evidence required to establish therapeutic vulnerabilities.

title: Crystallographic fragment screening in cancer and antiviral drug discovery: from electron density to translational outcomes.
authors: Balikci, Esra; Grimes, Jonathan M
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) provides an experimental starting point for small-molecule discovery by defining a fragment's binding site, pose and routes for chemical elaboration. By establishing a structural hypothesis before major medicinal-chemistry investment, CFS reduces early uncertainty and the risk of pursuing a binding mode inferred from activity or modeling but not supported by experimental structural evidence. AREAS COVERED: This review examines how CFS advances fragments into lead series, preclinical candidates and clinical molecules. Oncology examples include kinase inhibitors, the PHIP2 bromodomain, the transcription factor brachyury and the metabolic enzyme PYCR1. Antiviral examples include viral proteases, polymerases, the influenza PA endonuclease and the SARS-CoV-2 immune-evasion protein Mac1. It also considers the practical requirements and limitations of CFS, criteria for hit validation and prioritization, and how high-throughput crystallography, reusable structural datasets and computational or machine-learning methods can support chemical elaboration and translational decision-making. Relevant literature was identified through targeted PubMed searches conducted from March to September 2026, supplemented by reference-list screening of relevant primary studies and reviews. EXPERT OPINION: CFS is most powerful when it provides an experimentally grounded binding hypothesis early in discovery. It converts weak binding into actionable geometry, reveals ligandable pockets and supplies credible design starting points. Computational and machine-learning methods can extend this information by exploring chemical space, ranking fragment elaborations and supporting multiparameter prioritization, but they do not replace experimental determination of binding modes or functional validation. Future progress will depend on reusable structure-affinity datasets and tighter structure-design-synthesis-test cycles that connect crystallographic evidence to biological decisions.

title: miR-206 orchestrates breast cancer radiosensitivity through a SIRT1/p53 feedback loop: a network medicine modelling study.
authors: Fontinele, Djorkaeff O; Reiniger, Klaus A R; Azevedo, Arthur H D; Lima, Joao Paulo M S; Gupta, Shantanu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of breast cancer treatment, yet radioresistance limits its efficacy. miR-206 acts as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting SIRT1 and stabilizing p53. However, how these molecular components are organized within larger regulatory networks, and whether such network-level hubs can be therapeutically prioritized, remains unclear. RESULTS: Network modeling predicted a previously unrecognized double-negative feedback loop (miR-206  dash, vertical SIRT1  dash, vertical p53 --> miR-206) that functions as a predicted bistable switch, driving mutually exclusive commitment to either a radiosensitive (apoptotic) or a radioresistant (proliferative) fate. Monte Carlo simulations revealed that opposite perturbations of this circuit consistently drove the system toward the corresponding stable attractor. Edge disruption analysis identified the miR-206/SIRT1 and p53/miR-206 interactions as essential for maintaining bistability, while ATM exerted p53-dependent context-specific effects. Model predictions were consistent with independent experimental observations that miR-206 overexpression suppresses SIRT1, enhances p53 acetylation, and increases radiosensitivity. CONCLUSIONS: This network medicine framework identifies the miR-206/SIRT1/p53 bistable switch as a key regulatory module governing cell-fate decisions in breast cancer radioresistance. The model provides a systems-level platform for prioritizing experimentally testable therapeutic strategies to overcome radioresistance.

title: Bioinformatics Analysis to Reveal Potential Targets of Huntington's Disease.
authors: Yang, Shu; Xu, Xinjie; Liu, Weida; Zhang, Shuyang
