abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease resulted from the expansion of CAG repeats in huntingtin (HTT) gene and characterised by motor impairment, psychiatric disorders and cognitive decline. Currently, there are no available disease-modifying treatments. In this study, we performed an integrative analysis of HD datasets downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database using machine learning approaches, Mendelian randomisation (MR) and single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis to elucidate underlying disease mechanisms. The machine learning algorithms of LASSO, random forest and SVM-RFE identified the decreased ADRA2A in HD. In addition, MR analysis revealed HD-associated proteins such as LILRA4 and UBE2D1, associated with immune response and ubiquitination metabolism, respectively. scRNA-seq analysis further identified the transcription factors of SOX4 and ETV1 through SCENIC analysis. Pseudotime trajectory analysis highlighted heparan sulphate sulfotransferase activity, involving genes CHST11, HS3ST3A1 and HS6ST3 that drive cell differentiation. Moreover, cell-cell communication analysis demonstrated enhanced NRG1/3-ERBB4 signalling pathway in HD. This study presents multiple potential targets for HD treatment but further experimental validation is required to confirm their functional relevance.

title: MESP1 is transcriptionally activated by TFAP2A to promote malignant phenotypes and glycolysis in non-small cell lung cancer cells.
authors: Lv, Zhiping; Liu, Yang; Qiu, Rui; Zhang, Sheng; He, Wei
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer is a highly prevalent malignant tumor worldwide, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of cases and carrying a poor prognosis for patients. Mesoderm posterior basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor 1 (MESP1) encodes a bHLH transcription factor, and its mechanism in NSCLC remains incompletely understood. METHODS: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified through an integrated analysis of gene expression omnibus (GEO) datasets. Core genes were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and random forest (RF) machine learning algorithms, and their association with lung cancer risk was evaluated through logistic regression analyses. Western blot was used to detect protein expression. Cellular functions were assessed via colony formation, sphere formation, Transwell migration and invasion, extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), and lactate production assays. Upstream transcriptional regulatory mechanisms were validated using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and dual-luciferase reporter assays. RESULTS: A total of 106 common DEGs were identified, with SERTM1, PYCR1, and MESP1 selected through machine learning. Logistic regression confirmed MESP1 as an independent risk factor for lung cancer, exhibiting significantly elevated expression across multiple datasets. In vitro experiments demonstrated that MESP1 knockdown markedly suppressed colony formation, stemness, migration, invasion, ECAR, and lactate production, as well as glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1), hexokinase 2 (HK2), and pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) protein expression in NSCLC cells. Mechanistic studies revealed that transcription factor AP-2alpha (TFAP2A) directly bound to the MESP1 promoter to activate its transcription, and MESP1 mediated the promotion effects of TFAP2A in vitro. CONCLUSION: MESP1 is highly expressed in NSCLC and transcriptionally regulated by TFAP2A. These findings unveil a novel TFAP2A/MESP1 regulatory axis in NSCLC that promotes malignant phenotypes and glycolysis. This axis may provide a potential molecular basis for the development of targeted strategies, although further in vivo validation is warranted.

title: A Novel Phenolic From the Heartwood of Cotinus coggygria Scop. With Potential Neuroprotective Effects: In Silico and In Vitro Studies.
authors: Meng, Caiwen; He, Yi; Wang, Zijia; Bai, Hongyun; Wang, Ruyi; Wang, Xiaoliang; Zhao, Chunlai; Li, Meichen
abstract: Seven known phenolic compounds (2-8) along with one new phenolic compound (1) were isolated from the heartwood of Cotinus coggygria Scop. (Anacardiaceae). Among them, compounds 3-5 are reported from the genus Cotinus for the first time, while compounds 2 and 6-8 are reported from the family Anacardiaceae for the first time. The structure of the new compound was elucidated by detailed spectroscopic analysis, including HR-ESI-MS, 1D, and 2D NMR experiments. In vitro assays showed that compound 1 attenuated glutamate-induced oxidative injury in HT22 cells (EC(50) = 3.852 microM, MTS assay) and inhibited TNF-alpha-induced NF‑kappaB activation in 293T luciferase reporter cells. Molecular docking suggested that compound 1 may bind to IKKbeta, consistent with the observed NF‑kappaB inhibition. Preliminary structure-activity relationship trend analysis indicated that compounds possessing a 6''-O-rhamnose-containing disaccharide moiety (6-8) showed stronger apparent protective activity than the 6''-O -galloyl derivatives (1-5) under the present assay conditions. These preliminary findings suggest that cotinusin A (1) may warrant further investigation for its potential against glutamate-induced oxidative neuronal injury. However, whether the observed NF‑kappaB inhibitory activity translates into anti-neuroinflammatory effects in relevant models remains to be determined, and further mechanistic and in vivo studies are needed to establish its therapeutic potential.

title: TEAD as a druggable target in Hippo signaling: Structure-based discovery of small-molecule inhibitors.
authors: Prasad, Monisha
abstract: The Hippo signaling pathway is a well-conserved signaling pathway responsible for regulating tissue homeostasis, organ size, proliferation, apoptosis, and stem cell renewal. The dysregulation of the Hippo signaling pathway, specifically abnormal activation of the YAP/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional complex, has become a key player in initiating, promoting, metastasizing, and acquiring resistance to therapy in various tumors. Within the Hippo signaling pathway, transcription factors of the TEAD family have become the focus of growing interest as potential drug targets due to their status as the downstream mediators that convert oncogenic signals into transcription programs that ensure cancer cells' viability and proliferation. Thanks to advances in structural biology, the molecular structures of the TEAD proteins, such as the very well-conserved hydrophobic binding pocket and YAP/TAZ interaction site, have been revealed, making it possible to develop effective drugs rationally. Such drugs may inhibit TEAD proteins by preventing their post-translational modifications, blocking protein-protein interactions, or altering their conformation. Additionally, the development of computer-based methods, such as virtual screening based on structure, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and drug discovery assisted by artificial intelligence, has significantly contributed to the improvement of TEAD inhibitor selection and optimization. Some of the identified inhibitors exhibit promising efficacy in preclinical experiments, whereas the first TEAD inhibitors have already started entering clinical trials. In this article, we will briefly discuss recent discoveries in the field of structural biology of TEAD, analyze current methods of structure-based drug discovery, examine the pharmacology of emerging inhibitors of TEAD, and address some current limitations and future perspectives in TEAD inhibition.

title: Multiple domains of Matɑ1 transcription factor contribute to binding site specificity
authors: Emily Knisely-Durham; Simone M. Giovanetti; Meru J. Sadhu
abstract: Among homologous transcription factors with the same function, DNA-binding specificity can diverge. Matɑ1 is a high mobility group (HMG) box transcription factor in budding yeast whose Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans homologs regulate ɑ-specific genes but bind distinct cis -regulatory sequences. To identify the protein features underlying this divergence, we generated structure-guided chimeras and measured their activity using species-specific reporters. Replacing any of the four Matɑ1 regions reduced activation of the S. cerevisiae reporter, while all chimeras retained activity on the C. albicans reporter. Thus, all four regions of Matɑ1 – not just the HMG box domain – are important for sequence specificity.

title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
authors: Yangfang Xiong; Jiwu Ren; Xiaoxu Wei; Xiaoyu Li; Jiayi Li; Wensheng Wei
abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

title: Contrastive Learning Improves Generalization on M2OR Olfactory Binding Dataset
authors: Logan Snider; Oliver Nakano-Baker; J. Devin Mackenzie
abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.

title: Beyond Direct Binding: Serotonin Rewires Model Brain Plasma Membrane-Mediated Communication Pathways in Y4R
authors: Somdatta Paul; Pooja Sharma; Samapika Sahu; Ananya Debnath
abstract: Serotonin, an endogenous neurotransmitter, modulates pancreatic polypeptide (PP) recognition by the neuropeptide Y4 receptor (Y4R), a mechanism relevant to altered serotonergic signaling associated with metabolic disorder and anxiety. Although recent experiment demonstrates serotonin modulated PP dissociation kinetics of Y4R through membrane allostery, the molecular mechanism of serotonin-induced lipidomic reorganization of the brain plasma membrane (BPM) relevant for Y4R activation is unknown. To this end, a total of 825.9 ns long all-atom molecular dynamics simulations at 310 K elucidate the concentration-dependent coupling between serotonin partitioning, selective lipid reorganization, and PP-binding and Y4R activation relevant intra-receptor communication in a heterogeneous, asymmetric model BPM. In the absence of serotonin, Y4R preferentially associates with the anionic lipids. Serotonin preferentially localizes at the lipid–water interface over the PP-binding and activation-associated regions of Y4R. At 6 mM, serotonin preferentially contacts phosphocholine species depleted from Y4R, whereas at 50 mM, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate dominates both micro-environments. These changes align with the selective remodeling of lipid networks, enhanced lipid-chain ordering, and modest bilayer compaction. Weighted implementation of suboptimal paths analysis reveals concentration-dependent reorganization of communication pathways between experimentally implicated PP-binding and activation-associated Y4R residues. Collectively, these findings connects serotonin dependent selective lipid redistribution to altered intramolecular communication between Y4R residues associated with PP binding and G-protein coupling, and provide a framework for future experiments investigating membrane-mediated neuromodulation and neuronal signaling. These findings provide a basis for exploring lipid-targeted pharmacology as a complementary strategy to modulate GPCR allostery by altering membrane composition rather than directly targeting the receptor.

title: KH1 Domain of Poly C Binding Protein 1 (PCBP1) Interacts with Utrophin-A mRNA and Modulates Utrophin-A Expression in Mouse Myoblasts
authors: Doel Pal; Arka Bagchi; Subhanwita Das; Gargi Ghosh; Soumyak Pal; Shreya Saha; Chhanda Sarkar; Utpal Basu
abstract: Utrophin upregulation is an attractive strategy to ameliorate Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Here, we investigated whether the murine poly(C)-binding protein 1 (PCBP1) directly interacts with the utrophin-A mRNA, and how the interaction shapes the fate of utrophin-A in muscle cells. As no experimentally validated structure of the murine PCBP1 is available, AlphaFold2 was utilized to predict the structure of the full-length protein and the KH1-KH2 domain of the protein. The more stable and reliable model of the KH1-KH2 domain of PCBP1 was then docked with the 5′UTR of the utrophin-A mRNA, and the top-ranked docked complex was utilized for MD simulation to identify the most stable hydrogen bond-forming amino acid residues from PCBP1. ITC showed a thermodynamically favorable spontaneous interaction between the full-length PCBP1 and the 5′UTR of utrophin-A mRNA, but the deletion mutant of PCBP1, lacking the predicted contact region, failed to exhibit any interaction. This observation was also confirmed by an RNA-immunoprecipitation assay in C2C12 cells. However, the mutant PCBP1 was unable to alter the expression of the utrophin-A in the C2C12 cells. In cells, PCBP1 overexpression lowered utrophin-A expression, while shRNA knockdown produced reciprocal increases. A 5′UTR-luciferase reporter mirrored this observation. Finally, subcellular fractionation showed that PCBP1 promotes nuclear retention of utrophin-A transcripts and reduces their cytoplasmic availability, with reciprocal shifts upon PCBP1 knockdown. Considering earlier work on PCBP2, our data suggest both paralogs recognize the same 5′UTR element, and the KH1-dependent interaction represses utrophin-A by coupling nuclear retention to reduced protein output. Thus, the PCBP1-5′UTR interaction emerges as a potent target for utrophin de-repression in DMD.

title: PARP1-mediated PARylation of SPRTN restrains its DNA-protein crosslink repair activity
authors: Ayesha Rahman; Veronika Quevedo; Martin Garcia; Andrew Rhiner; Quincee Simonson; Estella Perez; Jaime Lopez-Mosqueda
abstract: SPRTN is a DNA-dependent metalloprotease that resolves DNA-protein crosslinks, but how its activity is restrained on chromatin remains unclear. Here we show that SPRTN is PARylated in a PARP1- and HPF1-dependent manner. Mass spectrometry datasets identify seven modified residues in the C-terminal region, and substituting them (SPRTN-PARless) strongly reduces PARylation. The Nudix homology domain is required for SPRTN to interact with PARP1 and for efficient PARylation. SPRTN-PARless accumulates faster and to higher levels at laser-induced DNA damage than wild-type SPRTN. PARylation reduces single-stranded DNA binding of both cell-derived and purified SPRTN, and PARG treatment reverses this effect for cell-derived protein. SPRTN-PARless shows increased autocleavage and accelerates clearance of camptotheci-induced TOP1 cleavage complexes. These findings suggest that PARylation acts as negative feedback on SPRTN after its PAR-dependent recruitment, restraining its DNA engagement and proteolytic activity.

title: Direct NMR evidence for transient binding of the vesicular SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 to the α-synuclein C-terminus
authors: Sophia Werner; Tobias Stief; Celina M Schulz; Katharina Vormann; Robin Backer; Marie P Schutzmann; Lothar Gremer; Wolfgang Hoyer; Nils-Alexander Lakomek
abstract: The protein α-synuclein (α-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the α-synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of α-synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the α-synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (μs-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling α-synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of α-synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.

title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
authors: Schmidt AW; Rosendahl J; Laumen H; Ossowski S
abstract:
Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,421,183 common variants and publicly available.

Abstract Figure

Graphical Abstract. eQIF is a novel score for predicting the gene-regulatory impact of variants. eQIF is based on the top 20 principal components (PCs) from the publicly available precomputed Enformer deep-learning chromatin predictions overlapping common gnomAD variants. The PCs were provided to an isolation forest to learn global density within the multi-dimensional feature space. After training the model, it was applied to predict a global anomaly score (eQIF) for all gnomAD variants. eQIF was finally used for fine-mapped variant classification, functional variant discovery and precise prioritization of highly informative TFBS positions. title: Enhanced Quantum Simulations Reveal Conformation-Controlled, Site-Resolved Proton Binding in Biliverdin
authors: Eleftherios Mainas; Kaiyi Tong; Elisa Pieri
abstract: For a molecule with several titratable sites, a measured pKa reports a change in the number of bound protons, but not the population of each tautomer. The biological chromophore biliverdin (BV) is a longstanding example: the protonation of its four pyrrole nitrogens controls its photoactivity, yet the reported pKa values vary by about two units, and ring C is typically assumed deprotonated in neutral BV without a site-resolving measurement. BV is also flexible, so its protonation microstates and its conformers form coupled ensembles: the shape of the molecule changes how tightly it binds the proton. Here, we compute the macroscopic pKa of BV in explicit water and the populations of its four neutral tautomers, from the site-resolved pKa of the four rings. Enhanced quantum-mechanical simulations follow a proton into bulk water, and the free energies of proton transfer between rings and of ring rotation connect all protonation states in one thermodynamically consistent network. In the locked-helix conformation that dominates in water, BV has a macroscopic pKa of 4.0, and its four nitrogens are almost equally basic (site pKa values of 4.5 for rings B and C and 4.9 for rings A and D). No single tautomer dominates: the tautomers deprotonated at rings B and C each make up 36% of neutral BV, and those deprotonated at rings A and D 14% each. Opening the helix at ring D, as in bacteriophytochromes, raises the macroscopic pKa to 6.4 and shifts the neutral form almost entirely to the ring B (71%) and ring C (27%) tautomers. The conformation of BV thus controls its proton binding more than the choice of ring.

title: From a Tight-Binding Hessian to an AMBER Iron-Sulfur Site: A Rubredoxin Stress Test
authors: Devashish Das; Anurag Kumar
abstract: Parameterized bonded metal sites represent the lowest cost option for molecular dynamics (MD) studies of metalloproteins. However, their quality depends entirely upon the underlying quantum computation and validation. Here, we have asked whether it is possible to generate reliable AMBER force field parameters for a rubredoxin Fe-S4 active site from an extended tight-binding (xTB-family) Hessian. The Hessian derived from a 49-atom cluster was projected using the Seminario method to give parameters for Fe-S and S-Fe-S interactions. The active site was then solvated explicitly, and three 100 ns trajectories were generated. The entire process was performed end-to-end. The trajectories all maintained the protein secondary structure (RMSD Cα mean 1.2-1.6 Å). Two of the trajectories maintained a tetrahedral iron site, while one did not. At around 31.4 ns, the mean Fe-S bond length increased from 2.41 to 2.63 Å, and the deviation from tetrahedral geometry increased from 8.8 to 43.5°. Two cysteine sulfur atoms also approached each other to a bond length of 2.04 Å. None of these issues were identified using global measures. The parameters are reported along with the cause of failure, likely reasons, and missing provenance, meaning this is merely a proof of concept, not a validated force field.

title: Explainable ML force-field for evaluating protein–ligand binding energy using SO3LR
authors: Hamza Agha; Sergio Suárez-Dou; Adil Kabylda; Alexandre Tkatchenko; Andrea Volkamer
abstract: Accurate estimation of protein-ligand binding affinities remains central to structure-based drug design. Classical force fields neglect important quantum-mechanical effects, while quantum mechanical and semi-empirical methods remain impractical for large biomolecular systems. Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) offer an alternative, but their performance may be inflated by training on protein-ligand complexes. Here, we introduce SO3LR-SF, a physics-based scoring framework that can be instantiated with any of the four pretrained SO3LR MLFF models, combining an equivariant message-passing network for semi-local interactions with physically motivated terms for short-range repulsion, electrostatics, and long-range dispersion. On PLA15 (15 active-site models), SO3LR-SF attains a relative interaction error of 2.1-5.8% against DLPNO-CCSD(T) references depending on the underlying SO3LR model, with SO3LR-T-M reaching 2.1%, the lowest of all tested methods. On the FEP benchmark (8 targets, 264 ligands), all SO3LR-SF variants achieve an average Spearman correlation of around 0.50, on par with the best semi-empirical quantum-mechanical method tested (0.47, GFN-FF) and with MMGBSA (0.44), and surpassing Glide (0.27). On the Wang dataset (8 targets, 199 ligands), the SO3LR-SF models reach around 0.59, matching the 0.59-0.62 range of molecular dynamics-based free-energy methods at a fraction of their cost. Each complex is scored in 3 s to 47 s on 12 CPU cores. An 8 Å trimming protocol reduces runtime threefold without loss of accuracy, and a restrained geometry optimization recovers ranking accuracy for targets with strained input structures. A multi-level explainability framework adds energy decomposition, per-atom energy contributions reported either for ligand or as 2D protein-ligand interaction maps, and 3D binding site visualization. We found that the polar SASA ratio of the binding pocket is predictive of electrostatic scoring performance, enabling estimation of ligand-ranking accuracy before scoring (r = 0.74-0.81 across models). Together, SO3LR-SF presents a fast, interpretable, and competitive scoring function for drug discovery that requires no experimental binding-affinity data for training.
